commentary.meaning: The run of weather-images continues, but the verse divides itself in half. The first two names give something: moonlight drawing up the ocean of a person's good fortune, and the rain-heavy cloud arriving over the peacock that is a devotee's mind. The second two take something away: the thunderbolt that shatters the mountain of disease, the small axe that fells the timber of death. Sky first, then earth; gift first, then demolition. Between them the verse completes a list that the previous verse had begun, since age was named there and sickness and death are named here. The second name is the hinge, and it is the only place in the whole run where the person praying appears at all. He appears as a peacock, which is to say as something that cries out and dances when the sky darkens but has no part whatever in bringing the rain. The images of the second half are Indra's own equipment — the dense cloud and the bolt both belong to the storm god of the Veda — and they have been quietly transferred to her.
commentary.history:
Abdhi, in the first name, is a small piece of poetic etymology worth unpacking: ap, water, plus dhi from the root dhā, to hold, so the ocean is the water-holder. Onto it the poet sets candrikā, moonlight, and behind the pairing lies a convention that Sanskrit poets treat as a fact of nature — the sea rises when the moon appears, swelling at the sight of it as a lover does. Purāṇic myth tightens the knot, since the moon was one of the treasures that came up when gods and demons churned the ocean of milk: the light that lifts the tide is the ocean's own child. Set this name beside the last name of the previous verse and the two form a pair, the sun against the darkness of age and now the moon over the water of fortune. Bhāgya itself picks up the thread as well. Where the earlier verse gave daurbhāgya, bad allotment, this one gives bhāgya outright, a whole sea of it.

The moon has a further and more technical life in this tradition. Śrīvidyā counts fifteen nityā goddesses, one for each lunar day of the waxing fortnight, and reckons Lalitā herself as the sixteenth digit, the kalā that never wanes and is therefore never subject to the fortnightly loss. Candrikā is the ordinary word for moonlight, and the verse is not making a technical claim; but a reciter who knows the nityā scheme will hear the name differently, as light from the digit that does not diminish falling on a fortune that consequently does not ebb.

The second name is built on two pieces of vocabulary that reward attention. Kekin is the peacock, and the word is derived from kekā, the technical term in Sanskrit poetics for the peacock's cry — the language has a separate noun for the sound each creature makes, and this bird is named simply after its noise. Ghanāghana is rarer: an intensive reduplication of ghana, which means compact or dense and, as a noun, a cloud. The doubled form names the heaviest kind of raincloud, the black wall of the monsoon's arrival, and the dictionaries record it also as an epithet of Indra and of an elephant in rut. Poets had a standing choice of birds for this scene. The cātaka is the usual one, said to drink nothing but falling raindrops and therefore to wait with its beak open through the hot months. The peacock is the other, and the peacock is chosen here because its response to the cloud is not thirst but display: it screams and it dances. The devotee's mind is being cast as the creature that answers the approach of the rain with an uncontrolled performance, having done nothing to summon it.

With dambholi, Indra's thunderbolt, the verse steps into Vedic mythology proper. The vajra is the weapon with which Indra split Vṛtra, the serpent who lay across the mountain holding back the waters, so that the rivers ran free — the central act of the Ṛgveda's Indra hymns, and the reason the cloud in the preceding name and the bolt in this one belong to a single complex rather than to two. Later mythology adds that the weapon was fashioned from the bones of the sage Dadhīci, who gave up his body when the gods needed something hard enough to kill Vṛtra with. The specific application to mountains has its own story: the mountains once had wings and flew, until Indra cut the wings off with the vajra to hold them still, and Maināka alone escaped by hiding in the sea, a tale Maināka himself tells Hanumān in the Rāmāyaṇa when he rises out of the water to offer him rest. Disease piled up like a mountain is therefore not simply broken, it is grounded.

The last name deflates its own object, as the cotton and the gale did in the previous verse. Kuṭhārikā is a diminutive: not the great axe but the hatchet, the household tool. Death is dāru, sawn timber. That the founder-figure of one strand of this tradition is Paraśurāma, the axe-bearing brahmin to whom the Paraśurāmakalpasūtra is attributed, gives the image a resonance in Śrīvidyā circles; the name itself makes no such claim, and I would not press it further than a resonance.
commentary.practice:
The two lines behave completely differently and need to be learned separately. In the first line the names are uneven — six syllables for bhāgyābdhicandrikā and ten for bhaktacittakekighanāghanā — so the caesura at the eighth syllable falls inside the second name, two syllables after it begins. Do not breathe there. The whole of the first line has to be carried on one breath, or the second name will be split after bhakta into something that means nothing.

The second line is the opposite: two names of eight syllables each, dividing exactly at the caesura. What hides the division is sandhi. Rogaparvatadambholiḥ ends in a visarga, and a visarga preceded by i and followed by a voiced sound becomes r, so the printed text runs dambholir mṛtyudārukuṭhārikā and looks like one enormous compound. It is two names, and the r that appears to join them belongs to the first. Knowing that is the difference between reciting the line and reciting a sound.

Ghanāghanā is the hardest thing in the verse to say cleanly. Both gha syllables are voiced aspirated velars, one sound each and not g followed by h, and under speed they collapse into ga-na-ga-na, which loses both the word and the thunder the reduplication is imitating. Slow the second half of that name down until each gha has audible breath in it. Elsewhere: ābdhi has b and dh together, both voiced, the second aspirated; dambholi has the labial nasal followed by aspirated bh; kuṭhārikā has ṭh, a retroflex stop with breath after it, nothing like the th of English "thin"; and mṛtyu opens with the short syllabic ṛ, the same vowel that caused trouble in vṛṣṭiḥ in the previous verse.

The archanā forms hold a genuine oddity. Three of the four are regular feminine datives — bhāgyābdhicandrikāyai namaḥ, bhaktacittakekighanāghanāyai namaḥ, mṛtyudārukuṭhārikāyai namaḥ. The third is not. Dambholi is a masculine noun standing in apposition to the goddess, and the namāvalī as printed here keeps its masculine dative: rogaparvatadambholaye namaḥ, with the ending -aye rather than -yai. Usage varies on this point between printed namāvalīs, and reciters who have been producing -āyai automatically for four hundred names will need to slow down and think. It is one of the small places where the hymn declines to be regular.

What the verse asks is set by its middle name. The peacock does not fetch the monsoon and cannot. It has a relationship to the rain that is entirely one of response — it hears the thunder, it cries, it opens the tail — and the poet has put the devotee's mind in exactly that position. Nothing in the verse suggests that recitation causes the thunderbolt to fall on the mountain of disease. What it offers instead is the description of a temperament: a mind that recognizes the change in the air. Chanted at a sickbed, which is where this verse tends to be chanted, that is a more sober promise than it first appears, and a more durable one.

crossReferences.deva: हिरण्यवर्णां हरिणीं सुवर्णरजतस्रजाम् । चन्द्रां हिरण्मयीं लक्ष्मीं जातवेदो म आ वह ॥
crossReferences.iast: hiraṇyavarṇāṃ hariṇīṃ suvarṇarajatasrajām | candrāṃ hiraṇmayīṃ lakṣmīṃ jātavedo ma ā vaha ||
crossReferences.translation: Golden of hue, tawny, wearing garlands of gold and silver, bright as the moon, made of gold — bring Lakṣmī to me, O knower of all that is born.
crossReferences.relevance: The oldest prayer for fortune in the tradition, and it already fastens fortune to lunar brightness: candrā, moon-like, sits in the same line as the gold. Bhāgyābdhicandrikā compresses the same association into a single compound, with the difference that the hymn does not ask for her to be brought — it describes the light as already on the water.

crossReferences.source: Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.3.2 (numbered 6.2 in editions that count the chapters straight through)
crossReferences.deva: यदिदं किं च जगत्सर्वं प्राण एजति निःसृतम् । महद्भयं वज्रमुद्यतं य एतद्विदुरमृतास्ते भवन्ति ॥
crossReferences.iast: yad idaṃ kiṃ ca jagat sarvaṃ prāṇa ejati niḥsṛtam | mahad bhayaṃ vajram udyataṃ ya etad vidur amṛtās te bhavanti ||
crossReferences.translation: This whole world, whatever there is, having come forth, trembles in the breath of life. It is a great terror, a raised thunderbolt. Those who know it become deathless.
crossReferences.relevance: The Upaniṣad turns Indra's weapon into an image of the absolute itself — a vajra held up, terrifying, and knowing it is what makes one deathless. The sahasranāma is doing the same transfer in the other direction, taking the bolt out of Indra's hand and giving it to her, and it is worth noticing that both texts move directly from the raised weapon to the overcoming of death, as this verse does in its final name.

crossReferences.source: Devī Māhātmya, chapter 11 (from the Nārāyaṇī hymn; verse numbering differs between editions)
crossReferences.deva: रोगानशेषानपहंसि तुष्टा रुष्टा तु कामान् सकलानभीष्टान् । त्वामाश्रितानां न विपन्नराणां त्वामाश्रिता ह्याश्रयतां प्रयान्ति ॥
crossReferences.iast: rogān aśeṣān apahaṃsi tuṣṭā ruṣṭā tu kāmān sakalān abhīṣṭān | tvām āśritānāṃ na vipan narāṇāṃ tvām āśritā hy āśrayatāṃ prayānti ||
crossReferences.translation: Pleased, you take away every sickness without remainder; angered, you take away all that is desired. For those who have taken refuge in you there is no calamity, and those who have taken refuge in you become themselves a refuge for others.
crossReferences.relevance: The scriptural warrant for rogaparvatadambholiḥ, and blunter than the sahasranāma is willing to be. The Devī Māhātmya makes the removal of disease conditional on her being pleased and states the other possibility in the same breath; the hymn drops the condition and keeps only the bolt. The last line is also the answer to the peacock: what the sheltered creature eventually becomes is shelter.

references.title: An Anthology of Sanskrit Court Poetry: Vidyākara's Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa
references.author: tr. Daniel H. H. Ingalls (Harvard Oriental Series 44, 1965)
references.note: Go to the section on the rains. Several dozen short poems on the arrival of the monsoon, with peacocks and cātakas in almost all of them, and Ingalls's introduction explains how a convention of this kind functions — not as description of a bird but as a fixed emotional shorthand. It is the fastest way to understand what the second name of this verse expects its audience to already feel.

references.title: The Rig Veda: An Anthology
references.author: tr. Wendy Doniger O'Flaherty (Penguin, 1981)
references.note: For the vajra. The Indra hymns translated here, particularly the killing of Vṛtra and the release of the waters, are the source of everything the word dambholi carries. Read two or three of them and the pairing of cloud and thunderbolt in this verse stops looking like two unrelated images.

references.title: The Transport of Love: The Meghadūta of Kālidāsa
references.author: tr. Leonard Nathan (University of California Press, 1976)
references.note: A poem in which a raincloud is the protagonist, and the most sustained treatment in Sanskrit of what the monsoon means to those waiting for it. Not a source for this verse, but the best available preparation for reading it, since the sahasranāma is borrowing a whole atmosphere in the space of one compound.

references.title: A Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: Monier Monier-Williams
references.note: Worth opening specifically for ghanāghana and dambholi, two words that a reader will not meet often. The entries show the intensive reduplication in the first and the range of names Indra's weapon goes by in the second, and they make clear that the poet reached for uncommon vocabulary here rather than the ordinary megha and vajra.

references.title: Lalitā Sahasranāma (traditional recitation)
references.author: Bombay Sisters, C. Saroja and C. Lalitha
references.note: The recording most South Indian households learn from, taken at a steady moderate pace with the word-divisions clearly articulated. Listen specifically to the second line of this verse to hear where a trained reciter puts the break in dambholir mṛtyu, which is the point at which most learners go wrong.
